hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? be honest: in a line, or a waiting room, how long before your hand reaches for your phone?
options: same here. this man saw it coming, centuries ago.
not bad. this story is about that minute.
then you’re rare. let’s see what you’re doing right.

steps.line: In France in the 1640s, a young man named Blaise Pascal built one of the first calculating machines, to help his father with tax sums.
Later, a gambler’s question about dice led him to help work out the mathematics of chance. And he watched his friends.
They gambled, they hunted, they rushed about at court. Take the hunter, said Pascal. He gallops all day after a hare.

steps.q: Pascal says: hand the hunter that hare as a gift, and he won’t want it. So what is he really after?
o: The noise and rush that fill his head
The skill of the catch, to feel proud
The company of his friends on the ride
steps.why: The bustle, Pascal says. It keeps him from thinking about himself. It was never about the hare.

steps.line: But hand him the same hare as a gift, and he wouldn’t take it. It was never about the hare.

steps.q: Pascal had a name for all this rushing about. What was it?
steps.why: Divertissement: diversion, literally a turning away. Hunting, gambling and chatter all turn our eyes away from ourselves.

steps.q: Pascal wrote that all human unhappiness comes from one single fact. What do you think it is?
o: Not knowing how to sit still
steps.why: One fact, he said: we can’t stay quietly in our own room.

steps.line: In an old translation of his notes: all the unhappiness of men arises from one single fact, that they cannot stay quietly in their own chamber.

steps.q: Pascal’s hunters and gamblers had money, friends and fun. Why does he still call them unhappy?
o: They lost too much at cards
steps.why: The rushing fills every gap, so they never have to sit with themselves. Pascal saw it in everyone, even kings.

steps.line: Pascal died at thirty-nine. His friends gathered his scraps of notes into a book, the Pensées, which means “thoughts.”
Today the hare fits in a pocket. A waiting room, a red light, a quiet minute, and the hand goes. The chase, again.
steps.label: today

steps.q: Pascal says even a king needs diversion. Why, in his notes, is a king surrounded by people all day?
o: To keep him safe from his enemies
To show the world his power
So he’s never alone with his thoughts
steps.why: The courtiers’ real job, he says, is to keep the king from thinking about himself. “A king without diversion is a man full of miseries.”

say: here’s what i love. pascal didn’t think the restlessness meant something was wrong with you. he saw it in everyone, kings included.
and he didn’t think the quiet room was empty. as a christian, he believed human restlessness is a hunger only god can fill. you don’t have to share his answer to take his advice: sit anyway.

steps.q: Your friend says, “I’m not restless, I’m just bored, so I scroll.” What would Pascal say the scrolling is?
o: A chase, away from the quiet room
A sign she needs a new hobby
steps.why: A chase. The hand reaches, not for the thing, but for a way out of the quiet.

today.say: today, once, when your hand reaches for something to fill a quiet minute, sit anyway. hands in your lap, one minute, nothing to chase. notice the pull, and stay.
options: good. a restless sit still counts as a sit.
it can be. pascal would say that’s the point. try thirty seconds.

sources: Pascal, Pensées 139 (Brunschvicg numbering), trans. W. F. Trotter (1910): “I have discovered that all the unhappiness of men arises from one single fact, that they cannot stay quietly in their own chamber”; the hare that hunters would not take if it were offered them; gambling, the court, the king without diversion.
Pensées 425 (Brunschvicg): the infinite abyss can be filled only by an infinite and immutable object, that is, by God himself.

Pascal’s calculating machine (the Pascaline, from 1642), made to help his father Étienne with tax calculations in Rouen; 1654 letters with Fermat on the problem of points, prompted by a gambler’s question (the Chevalier de Méré); died 1662, aged 39; the Pensées published from his notes in 1670.
